The story in one paragraph. The Indus script has a fixed writing direction and genuine positional syntax: a small class of signs ends texts, another opens them, and some never touch an edge. Every claim was tested against a random baseline. On the way we found and avoided a trap: the textbook direction test (forward vs backward model perplexity) is mathematically blind to direction. Finally, simulating Milestone 1's measured error rates shows that none of these findings would survive automated readings at today's 17% recognition accuracy. That justifies running on expert transcriptions and sets up Milestone 4.

1. Project context

The Indus script (~2600–1900 BCE) is undeciphered: there is no bilingual text, and inscriptions average about five signs. The project treats the inscriptions as a structured notational system and studies its regularities computationally, never claiming what any sign means. Signs are opaque labels such as P324.

Where Milestone 1 left off

  • Detection works: 99% coverage and 86% precision on 77 inscription strips.
  • Recognition does not: best 17% top-1 / 41% top-5 over 417 classes. There is a reproducible sim-to-real gap.
  • Milestone 2 therefore runs on expert transcriptions (the CISI corpus), as the M1 summary recommended.

What the proposal asks of Milestone 2

ObjectiveEstablish the direction of writing and calculate sign-pairing constraints.
Technical taskMap sequential transition frequencies; construct a Markov chain matrix; evaluate directional asymmetries by comparing text beginners vs text enders; apply Witten-Bell smoothing for unobserved pairings.
Deliverable“A directional statistical matrix verifying right-to-left syntax rules and tracking sign collocation indices.”
Cross-cutting goal“Analyzing how image digitization errors propagate down into downstream sequence analysis layers.”

2. Data, sourcing and key decisions

2.1 The corpus

SourceDigital CISI corpus — GitHub mayig/indus-valley-script-corpus, commit ad2f1e2 (MIT/Apache licence). A snapshot is included in the folder.
Content179 inscriptions (Mohenjo-daro M-1 to M-199), one JSON file each; every sign has an ID plus damage, line and uncertainty features.
Size after cleaning984 sign tokens, 181 distinct signs, 154 complete single-line texts.
NumberingParpola (P001…). It is not Mahadevan's 1–417, and the two cannot be mixed in one matrix.

2.2 Attempt to obtain the larger IM77 corpus

The proposal also points to Mahadevan's IM77 concordance at indusscript.in (~2,900 objects). It is a searchable, sign-in website. No public export of its inscription texts could be found, and an open-source toolkit that surveyed the sources reached the same conclusion. A zip supplied during the session turned out to be the 417 sign-image chart (the same Kaggle set M1 used), which holds no sequences. Decision: proceed with CISI, which the proposal itself lists. A second corpus (yajnadevam/indus-website, ~2,500 texts, its own numbering) exists and is noted as a future replication option.

2.3 The three decisions applied everywhere (Step 0)

DecisionRationale
Right-to-left reading order: each text is reversedThe corpus stores signs left-to-right as they appear on the impression, while the script is read right-to-left. After reversal, position 0 is the first sign read.
P000 = break, not a sign (19 cases in 18 texts)Deleting it would invent pairs that were never seen. Counting it would make "damage" look like the 4th most common ender. Texts are cut into segments at each break, and an edge next to a break is not treated as a genuine beginning or ending. 17 of the 19 breaks sit at a text edge, where seals wear.
Line breaks handled like breaks (7 two-line texts)How the two lines join is uncertain, so within-line pairs are kept but these texts' edges are not used for beginner/ender analysis.
Partly-damaged but identified signs kept (118 signs)The transcriber still recognised them.
⚠ Correction to the Milestone 1 summary. M1 §11 states that P324 opens 77 inscriptions and P385 closes 29. Those counts were taken in the corpus's stored (left-to-right) order. In reading order it is the reverse: P324 is the dominant ender and P385 the dominant opener. The M1 slides should be updated so that both milestones agree.

Step 2 — Text beginners vs text enders

Purpose: if direction did not matter, the two ends of a text would be interchangeable. A strong difference is the fingerprint of a fixed direction.

Beginner n share % Ender n share %
1 P385 29 17.5 P324 73 45.3
2 P378 10 6.0 P086 18 11.2

4 P011 5 3.0 P013 8 5.0
5 P123 5 3.0 P004 6 3.7

BeginningsEndings
Genuine edges166161
Distinct signs used8630
Top signP385 17.5% (95% CI 12–24%)P324 45.3% (95% CI 38–53%)
Entropy (unpredictability)5.63 bits3.22 bits

Flip test. The Jensen–Shannon divergence between beginner and ender distributions is 0.891 bits. In 10,000 versions where each text's direction was decided by a coin toss, the maximum was 0.418, so p < 0.0001. Random versions centre around ~0.33, not 0, because small samples always differ by chance. That is exactly why we compare against shuffled data instead of against zero.

Scope of the claim. The statistics prove the direction is fixed. Which end is the start comes from physical evidence (e.g. signs cramped at the left edge). Every result is consistent with right-to-left reading.

Checkpoint

  • ✓ Only genuine edges used (damage-adjacent edges excluded)
  • ✓ Wilson 95% confidence intervals reported
  • ✓ Permutation baseline instead of an assumed zero
  • ⚑ Chart fix: signs that are never at an edge first showed as empty rows. They are now labelled “never at either end — always in the middle”.

Step 3 — Transition counts and the Markov chain matrix

Purpose: a first-order Markov chain (bigram model) assumes that the next sign depends only on the current one. Rows = current sign, columns = next sign, cells = P(next | current). <S> (START) and </S> (END) markers are added only at genuine edges, so beginner/ender behaviour lives inside the same matrix.

Transitions counted1,123 = 796 sign→sign + 166 START→sign + 161 sign→END
Matrix size182 × 182 = 33,124 cells
Cells ever observed645 (1.95%)
Cells MLE sets to exactly 098.05%
Rows built from one observation73
Rows where MLE is “100% certain”84

Strongest rules (reading order):

  • P385 → P122: 28 of 33 (85%). The commonest opener is almost always followed by P122.
  • P332 → P324: 10 of 10.
  • P324 → END: 73 of 94 (78%). Otherwise mostly P324 → P013 (9×), and P013 → END 8 of 8, an alternative two-sign ending.
  • P217 → END 76%; P086 → END 53%.

Checkpoint

  • ✓ Every row sums to 1
  • ✓ Totals reconcile exactly with Step 0 (796 + 166 + 161 = 1,123)
  • ⚑ Label fix: a column described as “share of P324 occurrences” was really “share of observed predecessors” (2 occurrences follow a break). It was renamed.

Step 4 — Witten-Bell smoothing

Problem: MLE gives probability 0 to 98% of pairs, so one unseen pair zeroes a whole inscription. Witten-Bell: P(w|h) = [C(h,w) + T(h)·Puni(w)] / [C(h) + T(h)], where C = observations of the row and T = number of distinct successors. Each row holds back T/(C+T) for unseen pairs: the thinner or more varied the evidence, the more it holds back. Puni is itself interpolated with a uniform distribution, so no cell is ever 0.

RowCTHeld backReading
P38533513.2%well observed and consistent → stays confident (P385→P122: 85% → 74%)
P324941312.1%—
P122723432.1%very varied → stays open
START (openers)1668634.1%texts open in many ways
73 signs seen once1150%e.g. P265: MLE “100% P324” → WB 54% P324

Validation: 10-fold cross-validation by inscription (fit on 90% of texts, score the held-out 10%):

MethodHeld-out pairs given P = 0Perplexity (lower is better)
MLE (no smoothing)516 of 1,123 (46%)∞, fails in all 10 folds
Add-one (Laplace)077.3
Witten-Bell040.8

Perplexity ≈ the number of signs the model is effectively choosing between at each step. Uniform guessing over 182 options would give 182.

Step 5 — Directional tests and the directional rules matrix

5a. The perplexity trap (honest negative result)

Right-to-leftLeft-to-right
Training data, MLE (bits / transition)2.58612.5861 — identical
Held-out perplexity, Witten-Bell40.4340.39 (0.1% = noise)

A bigram likelihood is ∏ C(xt,xt+1) / C(xt). Reversing the text uses the same pair counts, only flipped, and the same sign counts, so the overall score is mathematically blind to direction. Any claim of direction based on it is empty. This is a direct exhibit for Milestone 4.

5b. Positional entropy, a direction test that works

Position from edgeAligned by FIRST signAligned by LAST signRandom-direction 95% range
15.312.944.36–5.04
24.85.605.25–5.68
35.325.205.10–5.47
45.385.015.10–5.47

The last sign is far more predictable than chance allows, while the first sign is more varied than chance. The opening's structure sits one position in (P385 → P122). Position-1 gap = 2.37 bits against a random maximum of 1.29, p < 0.0001 (128 complete texts with ≥ 4 signs).

5c. Directional rules

For each sign seen ≥ 8 times in complete texts: start/end rates against the chance rate (153 texts ÷ 857 signs = 17.9%), using a two-sided binomial test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q < 0.05).

ENDERSP324, P086, P217, P013
OPENERSP385, P378, P256
MEDIAL (avoid both edges)P122, P050, P120, P062, P060
No clear preference16 signs, mostly too rare to call

Headline examples: P324 at the end in 79% of its appearances; P217 87%; P385 at the start in 86%; P122 at an edge in 0 of 65 appearances (~23 expected by chance).

The full rules table is in Appendix A.

Step 6 — Collocation index (PMI)

Purpose: find pairs that occur together more often than chance predicts, as opposed to pairs that are common only because both signs are common. PMI(A→B) = log₂ [ P(A→B) / (P(A·)·P(·B)) ]; NPMI rescales it to −1…+1. Safeguards: a pair must be seen ≥ 3 times and pass Fisher's exact test (one-sided, BH-corrected, q < 0.05).

Distinct sign→sign pairs observed529
Pairs seen ≥ 3 times (scored)48
Significant collocations41
Frequent pairs (≥ 5) occurring in ONE order only17 of 22; 7 individually significant

Step 7 — Error propagation from Milestone 1

Purpose: answer the proposal's question on how image-digitisation errors propagate downstream. M1's measured error profile is injected into the clean transcriptions and the M2 analyses are re-run.

ErrorDerivation from M1Rate
Missed sign4.9 detected × 86% precision = 4.2 true hits of 5.6 true signs24.7%
Extra sign4.9 × 14% false positives = 0.69 per text ÷ 5.612.3% per true sign
Misreadbest recognition top-1 accuracy 17%83% at M1's level; swept 0–83%

Recognition accuracy was swept over 100 / 90 / 75 / 60 / 45 / 30 / 17%, with 50 random corruptions per level, both with M1's detection errors and with perfect detection.

FindingCleanAt M1's 17% accuracyPerfect recognition, M1 detection
P324 share of endings44%6%31%
Fixed direction detected100% of runs10%100%
Start–end gap2.46 bits0.12 bits1.22 bits
Collocations recovered100%0%44%
P324 still the dominant ender (share ≥ 25%)first lost at 75%
Fixed direction detected in ≥ 90% of runsfirst lost at 45%
Start − end gap ≥ 1 bitfirst lost at 75%
At least half of the collocations recoveredfirst lost at 100%
Key insight. Even with perfect recognition, M1's detection errors alone (25% missed, 12% extra) cut collocation recovery to 44% and halve the start–end gap: every missed or extra box breaks the pairs around it. Detection that is “solved” for finding signs is not good enough for sequence statistics. The direction signal is the most robust finding; fine-grained collocations are the most fragile.

Assumptions: misreads are drawn uniformly from the 181-sign inventory; reading order is correct; M1 rates carry ±~13 pp. Full table in Appendix D.

5. Honest negative results and limitations

  • The perplexity trap: forward and backward models score identically, so direction cannot be read from overall perplexity.
  • Raw PMI is misleading on small corpora; it needs a frequency floor and a significance test.
  • Small corpus: 179 texts from a single site. Every result carries random baselines or confidence intervals, and 16 of 28 frequent signs show no clear preference simply for lack of data.
  • Bigram model only: longer-range structure (e.g. the P385 → P122 opening formula as a unit) is left to Milestone 3.
  • No IM77 export available: an independent replication on a larger corpus is future work.
  • Not yet done (optional): a robustness re-run excluding the 118 partly-damaged-but-identified signs.

6. Links to Milestones 3 and 4

  • Milestone 3 (masked token prediction): the Witten-Bell matrix is the baseline predictor, and perplexity 40.8 is the bar to beat. The 19 P000 gaps are natural “predict the missing sign” test cases.
  • Milestone 4 (benchmarking hallucinations): two ready exhibits: (1) the perplexity trap, a confident metric that cannot answer the question asked; (2) error propagation, where a pipeline at 17% accuracy would “find” structure that is mostly noise.
